svg.text: Congestion Control Taxonomy: Open-Loop vs. Closed-Loop
Forouzan Section 24.3 / Tanenbaum Section 5.3 — Prevention Policies vs. Dynamic Closed-Loop Feedback

g.text: 1. Open-Loop (Prevention Ahead of Time)
Goal: Design protocols so congestion never occurs.
Policies implemented at source or destination without feedback:
A. Retransmission Policy
Use accurate RTO timers to avoid duplicate retransmission floods.
B. Window Policy (Selective Repeat)
Selective Repeat retransmits only lost packets; Go-Back-N wastes capacity.
C. Acknowledgment Policy
Delayed ACKs & NACKs reduce traffic load on return links.
D. Discarding Policy
Routers intelligently drop less critical packets (e.g., video B-frames).
E. Admission Policy (QoS)
Routers refuse new virtual connection setups if congested.
Note: Open-loop policies are static; they cannot respond to unexpected traffic surges!
2. Closed-Loop (Dynamic Removal & Feedback)
Goal: Detect congestion after it occurs and alleviate it.
Operates via closed-loop feedback mechanisms between nodes:
A. Backpressure (Hop-by-Hop)
A congested node stops receiving from its upstream neighbor;
pressure propagates node-by-node back to the original source.
B. Choke Packet (Direct ICMP)
Congested router generates a special control packet directly
to the source host ordering it to reduce transmission rate.
C. Implicit Signaling (TCP Loss Detection)
Source detects congestion autonomously via delayed ACKs,
increased RTT, or packet loss (3 dup ACKs / Timeout).
D. Explicit Signaling (FECN, BECN & ECN)
Routers set congestion notification bits directly in data packets:
• Forward (FECN) or Backward (BECN) / IP ECN (RFC 3168).
Modern Internet: TCP relies primarily on Implicit Loss Signaling + Explicit Congestion Notification (ECN)!
